visual.label: Connect and map
visual.effect: Branches show relationships.
visual.notice: Follow the shared trunk to the separate icons.

visual.label: Emphasise
visual.effect: A rule singles out words.
visual.notice: The underline makes a selected phrase stand apart.

visual.label: Frame
visual.effect: A border encloses one message.
visual.notice: The double frame gives the content a boundary.

visual.label: Organise
visual.effect: Rules organise a sequence.
visual.notice: Each chapter number belongs beside its horizontal rule.

visual.label: Divide
visual.effect: Rules separate editorial areas.
visual.notice: The news page uses lines between its sections.

visual.label: Decorate and direct
visual.effect: Repeated diagonals create rhythm and lead the eye.
visual.notice: The diagonal strokes occupy corners without enclosing the body text.

written.label: Short sentences
written.effect: Each full stop separates a complete movement.
written.notice: The three stops create a distinct pace; brevity does not always mean excitement.

written.label: A cumulative sentence
written.effect: The main clause arrives first; added details extend it.
written.notice: The sentence is already complete at the first comma.

written.label: A periodic sentence
written.effect: The main clause is delayed until the end.
written.notice: The first two pieces prepare the reader; the last supplies the main action.

written.label: Coordination
example: and cool air filled the room.
written.effect: A conjunction connects two independent clauses.
written.notice: Each side can stand as a sentence; and joins their movements.

written.label: Subordination
written.effect: A dependent clause gives the main clause a condition or contrast.
written.notice: Although introduces a clause that depends on the main statement.

written.label: A deliberate fragment
written.effect: A fragment can isolate an impression in narrative or dialogue.
written.notice: These are intentional fragments, not models of complete sentences for every task.

written.label: A question
written.effect: A question opens an unresolved route for the reader.
written.notice: The question mark identifies the sentence’s job; the text does not supply its answer.

written.label: A statement
written.effect: A statement gives the reader information.
written.notice: The full stop closes a complete statement.

written.label: An instruction
written.effect: An instruction asks someone to do something.
written.notice: Open names the action. The subject you is understood.

written.label: An exclamation
written.effect: An exclamation adds a strong reaction to a statement.
written.notice: The words give the same information; the exclamation mark adds surprise in this example.

visual.label: Monochromatic
visual.effect: One hue varies in tint, shade, or lightness.
visual.notice: Each strip stays within one colour family.

visual.label: Analogous
visual.effect: Neighbouring hues create related variation.
visual.notice: The selected hues lie next to each other on this traditional wheel.

visual.label: Complementary
visual.effect: Opposite hues create a strong relationship of difference.
visual.notice: The wheel joins opposite sides. Intensity still depends on the chosen tones.

visual.label: Triadic
visual.effect: Three spaced hues distribute colour variety.
visual.notice: Three selected points form a triangle around the wheel.

visual.label: Warm and cool
visual.effect: Hue groups offer different palette directions.
visual.notice: Reds and oranges sit opposite blues and blue-greens; mood depends on context.

visual.label: Saturation
visual.effect: Muted and vivid colours have different intensity.
visual.notice: The hue stays while saturation changes.

visual.label: Value
visual.effect: Dark and light values change legibility and focus.
visual.notice: The hue stays while the swatches get lighter.

written.label: Intensity
written.effect: Radiant suggests light spreading out with greater intensity.
written.notice: The word art expands in light and detail.

written.label: Size made precise
written.effect: Tiny narrows the description toward a very small size.
written.notice: The richer word contracts rather than becoming bigger.

written.label: Connotation
written.effect: Deserted can suggest absence or abandonment in this scene.
written.notice: The wording adds an association beyond an unoccupied space.

written.label: A more specific verb
written.effect: Trudged describes walking with effort.
written.notice: The heavier, downward movement visualises the added sense of effort.

written.label: Sound in a reporting verb
written.effect: Whispered tells us how the words were spoken.
written.notice: The lower, quieter presentation shows the added information; this is a choice about delivery, not just decoration.

visual.label: Outline, fill, and cut-out
visual.effect: A shape can be drawn by its edge, its filled area, or the surrounding space.
visual.notice: The same circular outline appears in three different ways.

visual.label: Geometric shapes
visual.effect: Regular shapes provide recognisable building blocks.
visual.notice: Look for straight edges, circles, repeated angles, and symmetry.

visual.label: Organic shapes
visual.effect: Irregular curves create varied silhouettes.
visual.notice: These contours resemble flowing or natural forms rather than regular polygons.

visual.label: Shape as a symbol
visual.effect: A silhouette can carry a recognisable identity.
visual.notice: The marks remain distinct even without colour. Familiarity also matters.

visual.label: Text as a silhouette
visual.effect: Many small marks build one larger outline.
visual.notice: The digits follow the outer circular contour.

visual.label: Build an illustration
visual.effect: Facets combine into a recognisable figure.
visual.notice: Small geometric areas together suggest the head and torso.

visual.label: Decorative construction
visual.effect: Simple parts build a more elaborate sign.
visual.notice: Bars, circles, and arcs become a decorative numeral.

visual.label: Shape as pattern
visual.effect: A repeated shape makes a surface pattern.
visual.notice: The same angular unit tiles across the field.

written.label: Letter
written.effect: Date, greeting, body, closing, and signature give a letter a familiar form.
written.notice: The placeholder words can change while the layout stays recognisable.

written.label: Haiku template
written.effect: A compact three-line layout makes a haiku-style template visible.
written.notice: This shows layout. The traditional English 5–7–5 syllable pattern needs real words; three lines alone do not identify every haiku.

written.label: Limerick template
written.effect: Five lines, with shorter third and fourth lines, suggest the limerick’s familiar outline.
written.notice: AABBA is a rhyme plan. Placeholder text demonstrates the planned shape, not actual rhyme or metre.

written.label: CV
written.effect: A name, contact line, and organised experience sections make a CV recognisable.
written.notice: Repeated entries and dates give the information a scannable shape; CV conventions vary.

written.label: Advertisement
written.effect: A headline, focal image, brief message, and action line create one common ad layout.
written.notice: This is one useful template, rather than a single required form for all ads.

written.label: Newspaper article
written.effect: Headline, deck, byline, and columns give this article a news-page shape.
written.notice: The wide headline sits above narrower continuous reading columns.

written.label: Scientific article
written.effect: Title, authors, abstract, and organised sections create one journal-article template.
written.notice: This IMRaD-style layout is common in empirical research, but journal and discipline conventions vary.

written.label: Dramatic dialogue
written.effect: Speaker names and turns make a script recognisable.
written.notice: Indentation and repeated speaker positions distinguish turns from prose narration.

written.label: Concrete poem
written.effect: The arrangement of words makes a visible silhouette.
written.notice: The words widen through light and narrow toward here, making a leaf-like silhouette.

written.label: Oulipo snowball
written.effect: A rule makes each successive word one letter longer.
written.notice: Our original six-line example grows through 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 letters; punctuation is not counted.

visual.label: Environmental surfaces
visual.effect: A depicted surface suggests a material or environment.
visual.notice: Cloud, grain, cracks, and particles have different visible marks.

visual.label: Biological surfaces
visual.effect: Marks suggest living surfaces.
visual.notice: Stripes, spots, feather lines, and leaf veins organise the surface differently.

visual.label: Made textures
visual.effect: Designed marks can suggest a material or process.
visual.notice: Compare a swirl, camouflage, halftone dots, and brush marks.

visual.label: Natural pattern
visual.effect: Repeated structures can come from living or environmental forms.
visual.notice: The wing, cells, clustered forms, and scales repeat in different ways.

visual.label: Designed pattern
visual.effect: A repeat unit creates regular texture.
visual.notice: Check the repeated checks, tiles, and ornaments.

visual.label: A repeating motif
visual.effect: One repeat unit links the whole field.
visual.notice: Trace one houndstooth unit before looking at the complete pattern.

written.label: Alliteration
written.effect: Repeated initial /s/ sounds link the words.
written.notice: The highlighted beginnings return like notes.

written.label: Assonance
example: Low moans rolled over the road.
written.effect: The repeated vowel sound in low, moans, and rolled links the phrase.
written.notice: Listen for the shared /oʊ/ sound in a common pronunciation.

written.label: Consonance
written.effect: The repeated final /p/ sound links words with different vowels.
written.notice: The ends, rather than only the beginnings, carry the repeated consonant.

written.label: Abrupt clusters
written.effect: Stops and consonant clusters make this particular phrase sound abrupt.
written.notice: The /kr/ and /kl/ beginnings require a different articulation from long flowing vowels.

written.label: Flowing phrasing
written.effect: Longer vowels and connected phrasing support flow in this example.
written.notice: The connected word strips travel over one continuous wave.

written.label: Onomatopoeia
written.effect: Sound-evoking words make the event audible in imagination.
written.notice: The typography distinguishes small repeated taps from the sharper final sound.

written.label: Phrase cadence
written.effect: Phrase boundaries organise the sentence into a cadence.
written.notice: The returns follow the phrase groups, rather than a claim that all prose has a musical metre.

visual.label: Flat shape to form
visual.effect: Shaded faces make a flat outline suggest volume.
visual.notice: The second triangular figure has separate light and dark planes.

visual.label: Geometric forms
visual.effect: Planes and regular volumes suggest solid construction.
visual.notice: Look at the block letters and faceted structures.

visual.label: Organic forms
visual.effect: Curving volumes suggest softer or irregular solids.
visual.notice: Highlights and shading follow the curved surfaces.

visual.label: Facets
visual.effect: Changes in tone distinguish planes.
visual.notice: Adjacent triangular faces have different values.

visual.label: Surface ribs
visual.effect: Repeated shading follows the object’s curvature.
visual.notice: The ribs wrap around the volume rather than lying flat.

visual.label: Type with depth
visual.effect: Extrusion and shading turn a letter into an object.
visual.notice: The B has a front face, side faces, and a cast shadow.

written.label: Story arc
example: He asked his friend for help.
written.effect: A problem, growing difficulty, turning point, and outcome give events an underlying arc.
written.notice: The request changes what happens next; the ending answers the opening problem.

written.label: Chiasm
written.effect: Themes return in reverse order around a central event: A–B–X–B′–A′.
written.notice: Afraid returns as not afraid; help returns as helped. The story remains in logical order.

written.label: Framed narrative
example: I told my friend about the storm.
The rain came through our roof.
We moved the beds and stayed together.
written.effect: An outer situation encloses the story being told.
written.notice: The telling and listening frame the remembered events.

written.label: Flashback
example: Years ago, her father had given it to her.
Now she knew which door to try.
written.effect: A return to the past gives a present event new significance.
written.notice: Years ago moves back in story time; now brings the reader to the present.

written.label: Parallel story strands
written.effect: Alternating strands let separate actions develop before they converge.
written.notice: Mina and Ben occupy different strands until the shared final event.

written.label: Turning point
example: Then he heard a child crying.
written.effect: A decisive event changes the direction of the action.
written.notice: The middle event turns leaving into staying; it is not simply a decorative central line.

visual.label: Figure and ground
visual.effect: Occupied and empty areas can define the same silhouette.
visual.notice: Compare the dark capsule with the capsule-shaped opening.

visual.label: Separate and gather
visual.effect: Gaps change which marks belong together.
visual.notice: The separated marks become a gathered arrangement.

visual.label: Overlap
visual.effect: Shared areas imply layers and relationships.
visual.notice: Crossing bars create different occupied and empty spaces.

visual.label: Transparency
visual.effect: Partial transparency reveals shared areas.
visual.notice: Overlaps remain visible through the translucent marks.

visual.label: Shadow and layer
visual.effect: Shadows suggest which shape sits above another.
visual.notice: The shadow separates the front crossbar from the vertical bar.

visual.label: Depth through scale
visual.effect: Changing size and value can suggest distance.
visual.notice: The bars decrease in size or contrast across the sequence.

written.label: Ellipsis: trailing off
written.effect: An ellipsis can leave a spoken thought unfinished.
written.notice: The three dots allow the sentence to trail away; they do not state the missing ending.

written.label: Dash: interruption
written.effect: A dash can mark an abrupt cut-off.
written.notice: The second voice enters before the first thought is completed.

written.label: Paragraph break
example: He heard a voice inside. His hand fell.
written.effect: A blank interval can give the last action room and attention.
written.notice: The words stay in order; the gap changes their grouping and pace.

written.label: Scene break
example: The last train left the city.
At dawn, Mina woke beside the sea.
written.effect: A marked gap can signal a change of time or scene.
written.notice: The separated blocks belong to different moments.

written.label: End-stopped line
written.effect: A line ending and punctuation can work together as a stop.
written.notice: Each line ends with a completed sentence.

written.label: Enjambment
written.effect: A grammatical thought can continue over the line break.
written.notice: The line break does not end the sentence; the connection crosses it.

written.label: Omitted reply
written.effect: An unanswered question leaves a meaningful gap.
written.notice: The action is given, but his answer is withheld; several interpretations remain possible.

written.label: Parenthetical pause
written.effect: An aside can momentarily step out of the main sentence.
written.notice: The parenthetical remark adds information while the main sentence continues.

written.label: Reading between the lines
example: Mina glances at her guest’s coat.
written.effect: Literal words can support more than one possible implication.
written.notice: The context supports possible wishes or concerns; no one ghost thought is guaranteed.
ghosts: I thought we had more time.

written.label: Gesture and words
written.effect: An action can complicate the spoken message.
written.notice: The repeated folding may invite concern, but it does not prove what she feels.
ghosts: I don’t want to discuss it.

written.label: Indirect request
written.effect: Context can make a statement function as a request.
written.notice: Please close the window is a plausible inference, rather than the literal wording.

written.label: Possible irony
written.effect: The situation can make apparently positive words ironic.
written.notice: Tone would help confirm whether she is being ironic.

written.label: Understatement
written.effect: The wording deliberately presents less intensity than the situation suggests.
written.notice: A little contrasts with the large amount of water shown in the context.

written.label: Different knowledge
example: The key is inside the coat.
written.effect: A reader can know something that a character does not.
written.notice: The separate layers show reader knowledge and character belief.
ghosts: The reader knows where it is.

visual.label: Sans serif
visual.effect: Plain finishing strokes create one type treatment.
visual.notice: This R has no serif at the ends of its strokes.

visual.label: Serif
visual.effect: Finishing strokes change the letter’s detail.
visual.notice: Notice the serifs on the R’s stem.

visual.label: Slab serif
visual.effect: Broad serifs give the letter a different texture and weight.
visual.notice: The finishing strokes are thick and block-like.

visual.label: Rounded
visual.effect: Rounded corners soften the contour of the letter.
visual.notice: The outside and inside corners are rounded.

visual.label: Script
visual.effect: Connected, flowing strokes suggest a written gesture.
visual.notice: The R uses a looping stroke rather than a plain stem.

visual.label: Blackletter
visual.effect: Broken and angular strokes create a dense type texture.
visual.notice: The R is built from sharp transitions and ornamental strokes.

visual.label: Decorative and abstract
visual.effect: A letter can also act as an expressive image.
visual.notice: Decoration changes the inside and outside of the R.

visual.label: Anatomy
visual.effect: Named letter parts help us describe typography precisely.
visual.notice: The guides identify the stem, counter, serif, and reference lines.

visual.label: Functional typography
visual.effect: Type organises reading as well as displaying words.
visual.notice: Headings, columns, and scale give these pages different reading routes.

visual.label: Creative typography
visual.effect: Type can become a composition or image.
visual.notice: The letter forms are rotated, layered, or given depth.

written.label: Contrastive stress
example: She said she had seen HIM leave.
written.effect: Stress can correct which person was seen.
written.notice: The noun/pronoun is foregrounded; a different stressed word would change the contrast.

written.label: Italics for inner thought
written.effect: A writer can use a type treatment to distinguish a thought from narration.
written.notice: This is one convention for presenting thought, not a compulsory format.

written.label: Emphatic repetition
written.effect: A growing type treatment can represent increasing emphasis.
written.notice: The words repeat while their presentation becomes more forceful.

written.label: Different voices
written.effect: Distinct presentation can help a reader distinguish speakers.
written.notice: Turn position and type treatment mark the voices; fonts do not determine personality.

written.label: Quoted words
written.effect: Quotation marks identify words presented as someone’s wording.
written.notice: The quoted message is framed inside the surrounding narration.

written.label: Headings and emphasis
example: Mina packed a map, water, and a torch.
written.effect: A heading signals the topic and makes a section easier to find.
written.notice: The headline and body have distinct jobs; bold type alone does not supply an argument.

written.label: Register
written.effect: Formal and casual wording suggest different voices, just as type choices can.
written.notice: The informal idiom hand becomes the more formal assistance. The central request stays close.

visual.label: Shape difference
visual.effect: Unlike contours make a comparison visible.
visual.notice: A smooth circle sits above an angular shape.

visual.label: Value difference
visual.effect: Light and dark values distinguish marks.
visual.notice: The darker central form stands apart from the lighter surrounding marks.

visual.label: Scale difference
visual.effect: A size difference changes emphasis.
visual.notice: The same horizontal direction remains while stroke size changes.

visual.label: Order and disorder
visual.effect: An arrangement can contrast with another arrangement.
visual.notice: The upper squares form a grid; the lower squares are scattered.

visual.label: Type contrast
visual.effect: Differences in type treatment separate text roles.
visual.notice: Compare headings, body copy, and the quotation.

visual.label: Direction and type
visual.effect: Rotation and scale create strong visual differences.
visual.notice: Large horizontal words contrast with smaller rotated text.

written.label: Antithesis
written.effect: Opposed ideas in a matching clause pattern make the contrast clear.
written.notice: Empty and full occupy corresponding positions.

written.label: Juxtaposition
example: A busy road ran beside a quiet garden.
written.effect: Adjacent unlike images invite comparison.
written.notice: Busy and quiet are put close enough for the reader to compare them.

written.label: Long, then short
example: We walked along the wet path, past the empty houses, and down toward the river.
written.effect: A short sentence can land differently after a longer one.
written.notice: The unequal sentence lengths make the change of pace visible.

written.label: Although
written.effect: A concessive clause contrasts an expectation with what happens.
written.notice: Crowded and alone describe different sides of the situation.

written.label: However
written.effect: A connective marks a turn between statements.
written.notice: However signals that the second statement complicates the first.

written.label: Expectation and reversal
written.effect: A reveal can contrast with a reader’s expectation.
written.notice: Large and tiny are arranged as setup and reveal, rather than as a universal rule about surprises.

visual.label: Scale leads
visual.effect: Large marks can lead attention before small ones.
visual.notice: Follow the descending widths and weights.

visual.label: Colour leads
visual.effect: A tonal difference can prioritise selected marks.
visual.notice: The darker horizontal bars stand apart from the lighter vertical ones.

visual.label: Layer leads
visual.effect: Overlap and shadow distinguish foreground from background.
visual.notice: The crossbar appears in front of the vertical shape.

visual.label: Perspective leads
visual.effect: Depth cues arrange relative prominence.
visual.notice: The nearby-looking bars have more visual presence.

visual.label: Value leads
visual.effect: One darker item gains emphasis in a field of lighter items.
visual.notice: Locate the dark dot before scanning the rest.

visual.label: Depth leads
visual.effect: Sharpness and shadow separate one focus from the surrounding field.
visual.notice: The sharply visible bar contrasts with more distant-looking marks.

written.label: Point before support
example: The path beneath this tree feels cooler.
written.effect: A main point gives the supporting information a place to belong.
written.notice: The point, reason, and example have distinct roles.

written.label: Delayed main point
example: after a long walk in the rain,
written.effect: The main event can arrive after its preparation.
written.notice: The last part supplies the action that the opening has held back.

written.label: Background and foreground
written.effect: A subordinate clause can supply background for the main action.
written.notice: The background remains visible while the main action gains emphasis.

written.label: Known to new
example: The path led to a house.
The house had a red door.
written.effect: A returning element can carry the reader toward new information.
written.notice: Path and house return as the next sentence’s starting points.

written.label: End-weight
example: a heavy wooden box filled with old maps.
written.effect: A short opening can lead toward a longer information group.
written.notice: The longer object phrase sits at the end; this is one useful arrangement, not the only correct one.

written.label: Section headings
example: The station had one small room and a bench beside the window.
written.effect: A heading prepares the reader for the section beneath it.
written.notice: The section marker has more prominence than its supporting detail.

visual.label: Grid
visual.effect: Shared guides organise several kinds of content.
visual.notice: Compare the empty grid with the page placed on it.

visual.label: Text columns
visual.effect: Common edges help the eye enter and leave lines consistently.
visual.notice: The prose blocks follow the same column boundaries.

visual.label: Rotated axis
visual.effect: A composition can share an angled guide.
visual.notice: The headline and related material follow the same rotated direction.

visual.label: Vertical type
visual.effect: Aligned directions can also be vertical.
visual.notice: The tall words form related columns.

visual.label: Shared baseline
visual.effect: Different letters can share one reference line.
visual.notice: The letter sizes differ, but their bases meet the same guide.

written.label: Parallel verbs
example: She wanted to read the story,
written.effect: Matching grammatical forms organise a series.
written.notice: Read, understand, and explain share the same verb form.

written.label: Parallel clauses
written.effect: Corresponding clause patterns make a relationship easy to follow.
written.notice: The subjects and verbs sit in corresponding positions.

written.label: Related meaning
written.effect: Different words can develop a related image.
written.notice: Calm and still correspond in meaning without being identical grammar.

written.label: Contrasting parallels
written.effect: Corresponding positions can carry opposing meanings.
written.notice: The voices differ, but the two clauses form a related pattern.

written.label: Stanza correspondence
example: The sea saw it and ran away.
Sea, why did you run away?
Jordan River, why did you turn back?
Mountains, why did you jump like rams?
Hills, why did you jump like lambs?
written.effect: Descriptions return as questions about the same four images.
written.notice: The short adaptation and two-stanza teaching layout use Psalm 114:3–6; the source and context remain in the lesson.

written.label: A consistent list
written.effect: A series can share a consistent grammatical shape.
written.notice: The three -ing forms begin their items in the same way.

visual.label: Symmetrical balance
visual.effect: Visual weight is organised around a corresponding structure.
visual.notice: Inspect both sides and the larger page structure; they need not contain identical wording.

visual.label: Asymmetrical balance
visual.effect: Different objects can distribute visual weight without mirroring.
visual.notice: Compare the large image with the smaller type and objects.

visual.label: Radial balance
visual.effect: Objects are organised around a centre.
visual.notice: The repeated images lead around the central point.

visual.label: Weight through size
visual.effect: Size changes the distribution of visual weight.
visual.notice: A large circle has more presence than a small one in this example.

visual.label: Balance around an axis
visual.effect: A shared axis makes a distribution easy to compare.
visual.notice: Inspect the corresponding forms on either side of the guide.

written.label: Colon: explanation
written.effect: A colon can introduce an explanation of a complete statement.
written.notice: The second clause explains why the room grew quiet; clause lengths need not be equal.

written.label: Semicolon: related statements
written.effect: A semicolon can join related independent clauses.
written.notice: Each side is complete; the mark shows a close relationship without supplying a conjunction.

written.label: Paired clause pattern
written.effect: A matching grammatical pattern can balance two related actions.
written.notice: The parallel clauses distribute the actions between two people.

written.label: Comma after a dependent opening
written.effect: A comma can mark the boundary before the main clause.
written.notice: The first clause depends on the second. A comma does not always join two independent clauses.

written.label: Dash: a reveal
written.effect: A dash can foreground an added reveal.
written.notice: The second piece identifies the thing; it need not be a complete clause.

written.label: Periods: separate statements
written.effect: Separate sentences give each statement its own stop.
written.notice: This version is grammatical. It presents two statements rather than explicitly introducing an explanation.

visual.label: Grouped editorial content
visual.effect: Related items form readable clusters.
visual.notice: Pictures, labels, and text have local relationships.

visual.label: Clear picture–caption relations
visual.effect: Close placement supports the intended reading relationship.
visual.notice: The picture names sit near the matching pictures.

visual.label: Crowded without a clear order
visual.effect: Closeness alone does not guarantee clarity.
visual.notice: Different items share space without a consistent relationship.

visual.label: Scattered relations
visual.effect: Distance can make the intended association difficult to find.
visual.notice: The text and pictures are dispersed across the page.

visual.label: Gap between groups
visual.effect: A small inside gap and larger outside gap define groups.
visual.notice: Read the two clusters separately.

written.label: Paragraph focus
example: A rope lay beside the oar.
written.effect: A paragraph gathers details with a shared focus.
written.notice: Water details and boat details form two local groups.

written.label: Parenthesis
written.effect: Parentheses place an aside inside its host sentence.
written.notice: The paired marks keep the extra comment together while the main sentence continues.

written.label: Square brackets
written.effect: Square brackets can identify an editor’s inserted clarification.
written.notice: This original teaching quotation shows [Mina] clarifying she; the addition is visibly marked.

written.label: Apposition
written.effect: An adjacent noun phrase can rename or explain a person.
written.notice: Mina’s brother identifies Leo. The phrase stays next to the person it explains.

written.label: Pronoun and antecedent
written.effect: A pronoun links back to an earlier noun.
written.notice: It refers to a boat; the highlight makes the relationship visible.

written.label: A footnote
example: Mina marked the path¹ on her map.
written.effect: A reference marker links the reading to a nearby note.
written.notice: The matching 1 carries the association even when the note sits outside the sentence.

written.label: Quotation and commentary
example: “Meet me at dawn,” the note said.
Mina put it beside her bag.
written.effect: Related commentary helps a quoted message stay in its local context.
written.notice: The quote and immediate response form one short reading group.

visual.label: Repeat a motif
visual.effect: One recurring mark links a field.
visual.notice: A repeated circle is the shared visual unit.

visual.label: Regular rhythm
visual.effect: Equal intervals create a steady sequence.
visual.notice: The recurring objects have similar spacing.

visual.label: Alternation
visual.effect: Two recurring units create an alternating pattern.
visual.notice: Follow the change between green and gold.

visual.label: Progression
visual.effect: A repeated unit can change in a systematic way.
visual.notice: The circles grow while remaining circles.

visual.label: Consistent identity
visual.effect: Repeated style links different messages.
visual.notice: Colour, heading treatment, and divider position recur across the cards.

written.label: Anaphora
written.effect: A repeated beginning links separate statements.
written.notice: She remembered returns at the start.

written.label: Epistrophe
written.effect: A repeated ending links separate statements.
written.notice: By the river returns at the end.

written.label: Anadiplosis
written.effect: An ending returns as the next beginning.
written.notice: Fear makes the link between the two sentences.

written.label: Refrain
written.effect: A line returns at intervals.
written.notice: Still, we continued is the returning line.

written.label: Inclusio / bookends
example: We left the river at dawn.
At last, we returned to the river.
written.effect: A returning image frames the passage.
written.notice: The river occurs at both the opening and the close.

written.label: Motif
example: A red ribbon tied the box.
Later, a red ribbon marked the door.
She kept a red ribbon in her pocket.
written.effect: A recurring detail can connect different parts of a story.
written.notice: The ribbon returns in different situations; its larger meaning depends on the story.

written.label: Polysyndeton
example: We waited and listened and watched and hoped.
written.effect: Repeated conjunctions can give each action a returning beat.
written.notice: And links every item, rather than appearing only before the last.

visual.label: Remove decoration
visual.effect: Extra decoration can compete with necessary information.
visual.notice: Compare the ornament with the event details.

visual.label: Keep essentials
visual.effect: A useful reduction preserves the message’s job.
visual.notice: The event, time, place, and action are retained.

visual.label: Too little information
visual.effect: A minimal design can still fail its purpose.
visual.notice: The headline alone does not give the time or place.

visual.label: One clear route
visual.effect: One relevant path can explain a journey clearly.
visual.notice: The line leads from the entrance to the library.

visual.label: Purposeful whitespace
visual.effect: Room around the content can help its important parts stand out.
visual.notice: The surrounding area separates the message from the edge.

written.label: Cut filler
example: It is important to note that
written.effect: Removing an unnecessary opening brings the useful fact forward.
written.notice: The essential information remains.

written.label: Remove overlap
written.effect: Overlapping wording can repeat information already present.
written.notice: Planned already points ahead in this short example.

written.label: One precise verb
example: She made a quick movement towards the door.
written.effect: A precise verb can replace a longer description.
written.notice: Rushed combines movement and speed; it also makes the description more specific.

written.label: Direct actor and action
example: The door was opened by Mina.
written.effect: A direct subject–verb route can foreground the actor.
written.notice: The active version puts Mina first. Passive wording can be useful when the door is the focus.

written.label: Grammatical ellipsis
written.effect: A recoverable verb can be omitted from a parallel clause.
written.notice: The second clause borrows carried from the first; this compact form suits some contexts.

written.label: Keep the necessary reason
written.effect: A concise sentence should still retain the information the task needs.
written.notice: Removing the purpose would change what the reader understands.

written.label: Oulipo lipogram
example: Rain taps on old tin roofs.
written.effect: A chosen letter is excluded from the text.
written.notice: This original sentence contains no e. The restriction is a creative design rule, rather than a general rule of good writing.

visual.label: Inform
visual.effect: A timetable helps someone find information.
visual.notice: The session names, times, and rooms answer practical questions.

visual.label: Guide
visual.effect: A direction sign helps someone navigate.
visual.notice: The arrow and place name work together.

visual.label: Invite
visual.effect: An invitation needs details that make attendance possible.
visual.notice: Find the event, time, location, and next action.

visual.label: Prompt an action
visual.effect: A clear control makes the next step apparent.
visual.notice: The button wording identifies an action.

visual.label: Fit the viewing context
visual.effect: A visual must work where and how it will be read.
visual.notice: Consider the size, distance, and information needed.

written.label: Narrative
written.effect: A narrative follows particular events.
written.notice: The sequence forms a story route.

written.label: Explanation
written.effect: An explanation connects a cause and an effect.
written.notice: The causal arrow explains the relationship rather than only presenting two events.

written.label: Description
example: Light rested on a chipped blue cup.
written.effect: Description develops the qualities of a person, place, or object.
written.notice: The words add light, surface, and colour to one object.

written.label: Argument
example: Evening access could help students after work.
written.effect: An argument gives a position and supporting reason.
written.notice: The first sentence proposes a choice; the second supports it.

written.label: Instruction
written.effect: Instructions organise actions for someone to carry out.
written.notice: Numbering and imperative verbs provide a practical route.

written.label: Reflection
example: Now I notice the small details.
written.effect: Reflection can compare an earlier view with a changed understanding.
written.notice: Used to and now distinguish the two perspectives.

written.label: Inquiry
written.effect: An inquiry opens a question to investigate.
written.notice: The question asks for an explanation; it does not already provide one.

shape_core.goal: Recognise how visual outlines and document layouts give a message a form.

labs.label: Letter
text: Date, greeting, body paragraphs, closing, and signature.
labs.effect: The page groups a message around familiar letter conventions.

labs.label: Haiku template
text: Three compact lines. A traditional English haiku template often uses 5–7–5 syllables.
labs.effect: The line pattern is visible. Placeholder text alone does not establish syllables or poetic content.

labs.label: CV
text: Name and contact details, followed by grouped experience and education.
labs.effect: Headings, dates, and repeated entries make the information easy to scan.

manipulate.prompt: Match each document name to its placeholder-text template. Use the arrangement, rather than the words.
manipulate.reason: Dates and a signature identify the letter; three compact lines give the haiku template; dated sections give the CV; headline and action give the ad; columns give the news page; abstract and sections give the journal template.

transfer.prompt: Which page shape would best organise work experience, education, and contact details?
transfer.reason: The CV template groups experience and education under headings and places contact information near the name. The other shapes serve different jobs.

form_core.goal: Trace how an underlying story structure gives events depth and direction.

labs.label: Story arc
text: He asked his friend for help.
labs.effect: The request is a turning point; the outcome resolves the opening problem.

labs.label: Thematic chiasm
labs.effect: A–B–X–B′–A′: afraid and help return around the friend’s arrival.

labs.label: A story within a story
text: I told my friend about the storm.
The rain came through our roof.
We moved the beds and stayed together.
labs.effect: The present act of telling frames the remembered events.

manipulate.prompt: Build this short story: problem → difficulty → request for help → response → outcome.
tiles: He asked his friend for help.
manipulate.reason: The request changes the situation. The response finds the cause; the outcome answers the opening problem.

transfer.prompt: In this five-step chiasm, which sentence is the centre around which afraid and help return?
transfer.reason: The arrival is the central event. Afraid returns as not afraid; help returns as helped on either side.
